newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexicans vote in state poll amid fears of violence.
newsitem.headline: Mexicans vote in state poll amid fears of violence.

text.p: Mexicans began voting on Sunday in the troubled southwestern state of Guerrero amid fears of violence in local contests between a strongarm government and an increasingly angry opposition.

Watching the vote from a distance were thousands of army troops and armed rebels of the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR), a group which first appeared in this state and sees the vote as a test of government promises to clean up historically dirty elections.

The only initial report of trouble was the stabbing death early on Sunday of an opposition activist in the town of Altamirano, 95 miles (150 kms) north of state capital Chilpancingo. It was not clear if the incident was related to the elections.

Across Mexico, the election for new mayors and a state congress was being closely watched following a wave of violence between local members of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) and the mostly leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD).

PRD leaders have vowed to contest any outcome they consider the product of fraud and have already complained that the PRI used dirty pre-electoral tricks such as vote buying to keep its grip on power in the state.

In the town of Xochipala, 50 kilometres (32 miles) north of Chilpancingo, heated arguments flared when a local PRI leader and head of the town's voting station turned up drunk and did not want PRD members to help count ballots.

"It's always the same thing. The PRI wins no matter what happens. I think people are getting tired of this," said Florencio Garcia Martinez, a 48-year old construction worker in the nearby town of Zumpango.
Luciano Perez, an elementary school teacher in Zumpango, said people in his neighbourhood were offered free bags of cement if they could prove they voted for PRI candidates.
Army troops suspended counter-insurgency operations in search of EPR rebels over the weekend and were ordered to remain in their barracks during the vote.

Human rights groups feared many voters would stay at home following a massive mobilisation of army troops this summer to search for the EPR after a series of deadly attacks on police and army stations.
Although the army was temporarily gone from view, state police armed with automatic rifles and wearing bullet-proof vests roamed the streets in convoys early on Sunday.

The PRI was expected to win nearly all the races, including the state capital Chilpancingo and the posh tourist resort of Acapulco, despite an economic crisis and a series of political scandals that have cost it support across Mexico.
The PRI, which has ruled Mexico for 67 consecutive years, has overwhelming political power in the state, controlling 68 of the 76 town halls. The leftist PRD runs six towns.

PRI banners, swathed in the colours of the Mexican flag, festooned the streets of Chilpancingo over the weekend. The advertisements reminded voters of the EPR's deadly tactics in the state by featuring a giant dove next to the slogan: "Vote for peace, vote for unity."
Violence is common in Guerrero, one of Mexico's poorest states, where half the workers earn less than four dollars a day and nearly a third of the population is illiterate.
During state elections in 1989, 20 people died in post-electoral clashes between leftists and state police.

One possible trouble spot was the hamlet of Aguas Blancas, 60 kms (38 miles) from Acapulco. In June, 1995, state police massacred 17 leftist peasants there, causing former Gov. Ruben Figeroa to resign amid charges he ordered the killing.
